extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art critics, and educated readers interested in art theory/criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A set of normative principles and evaluative criteria for producing and judging landscape painting and art criticism, as argued by John Ruskin in the prefaces to Modern Painters. Emphasizes truth to nature, moral effect, technical fidelity, originality, and the qualifications of critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth to Nature / Fidelity to Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter must give the truth of Nature; no picture should be taken as a substitute for nature. 'The picture which is taken as a substitute for nature, had better be burned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should be founded on accurate observation of natural phenomena and render things as they are. Alteration, caricature, or invention that departs from the real characters of objects is an anti-pattern; works of the old schools that violate specific form are cited as examples of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of Specific Characters (Perfect Knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand style is based on 'the perfect knowledge, and consists in the simple, unencumbered rendering, of the specific characters of the given object, be it man, beast, or flower.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every change, caricature, or abandonment of specific character is destructive of grandeur and truth. The criterion demands precise understanding of each object's distinctive features rather than generalized abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of the Artist (Self-annihilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's power is proved by self-annihilation: 'The artist has done nothing till he has concealed himself,--the art is imperfect which is visible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful art makes viewers feel the subject rather than notice the artist's methods; visible technique or ostentatious display of skill is a defect. Example contrast: spectators who praise 'skill of the artist' rather than 'the perfection of nature' indicate a false school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and Spiritual Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape painting ought to speak to the heart, prompt devotion, and lift thoughts toward the divine; it should do more than amuse the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin criticizes existing landscape art for failing to 'teach one deep or holy lesson' and for becoming 'an exhibition of the dexterity of man.' The ideal picture should move and exalt, not merely display technical dexterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of Eye and Fidelity of Hand (Elementary Technical Merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary rules of art: merits attainable by accuracy of eye and fidelity of hand are foundational—art begins with accurate seeing and faithful execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin describes his work as treating 'the initiatory steps of art' and emphasizes that before higher, eclectic qualities, a painter must demonstrate accuracy in observation and in rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Artificialness and Self‑imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter should not 'take upon him to modify God's works at his pleasure' or 'cast the shadow of himself on all he sees' by imposing contrived combinations or impossible effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial arrangements, contrived combinations, and visible manipulation of nature are condemned. Anti-patterns include painters or critics praising 'invention' where it results in unnatural combinations or loss of individual object-character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality Validated by Nature (Dissimilarity as Positive Evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissimilarity from canonical models can indicate greatness: if a modern work 'can be shown to have the authority of nature on its side' then its difference from past works is evidence of higher power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss innovative manner or matter simply because it differs from the canon; evaluate whether it embodies truths grounded in nature. Ruskin warns critics who equate novelty with inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified Respect for the Ancients without Idolization
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect antiquity as a source of discipline and accumulated knowledge, but do not treat ancient works as models of absolute perfection or fetter modern advancement to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiquity should be a guide, not a jailer; the ancients' works may be imperfect in aspects and can be improved upon. Avoid using past excellence as a blanket reason to reject modern achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Idealization Must Connect to Real Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: If ideal or mythological elements are introduced, there must be a true and real connection between the abstract idea and the actual features of nature which originally modelled the conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealization that severs ties to real, specific forms is false. Mythological or spiritual figures must be coherent with the natural world; otherwise the link to meaning and beauty is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate by Evidence and Demonstration, Not Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical assertions should be 'grounded altogether on demonstrations which must stand or fall by their own strength' rather than on appeals to authority or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin likens his method to demonstration in Euclid; critics and artists should prefer verifiable observation and reasoned demonstration over mere citation of past reputations or rhetorical flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Response: Praise for Nature over Praise for Technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of good painting is that viewers leave with feelings about nature or the divine, not technical admiration: common visitors praise composition/skill rather than feeling 'the perfection of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spectators chiefly note the artist's dexterity, the work belongs to a 'debased, mistaken, and false school.' The ideal viewer response is silent delight or spiritual exaltation rather than technical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic Qualifications and the Limits of Popular Journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Good criticism requires knowledge and experience; newspaper critics who aim to mirror public feeling are unqualified to judge art properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin warns that many periodical critics are ignorant of art's canons, natural facts, and technicalities (examples: preferring inferior painters, misunderstanding simple terms). Anti-pattern: relying on reviewers who base opinion on readers' tastes or a week's superficial study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress and the Reception of Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine innovation will divide critics into factions: the conservative majority judging by precedent and the small minority recognizing new truths; reception of new masters may be hostile initially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect hostility from those whose judgment is rooted in precedent; recognition of a true innovator may require time and devoted study. This is a sociocultural criterion for evaluating the trajectory of new work.
